details.reason: CACDS runs the CJX civil-airplane case end-to-end, evidencing an integrated conceptual-design environment.
The CJX case uses ModelCenter's Boeing Design Explorer optimizer for DOC minimization, evidencing simulation-integration optimization.
CACDS provides a unified geometry-to-analysis-to-optimization workflow, supporting an integrated end-to-end design route.
CACDS is coupled with ModelCenter as optimization engine via defined inputs/outputs, supporting simulation-optimization integration.
CACDS exposes design variables, constraints, and objectives to ModelCenter, enabling optimizer setup.
ModelCenter includes DOC-minimization and other optimization templates, supporting objective-minimizing design workflows.
The DOC-optimized concept changes wing geometry, showing the optimizer applied within the design case.
A unified modular MDO framework integrates disciplinary modules into one optimization environment, supporting integrated aircraft optimization.
The MDO framework's Level 2 module optimizes configuration geometry with objective functions, supporting the optimization-environment route.
The MDO framework's Level 2 module optimizes wing layout and planform parameters, further evidencing optimization within conceptual design.
States the modular MDO framework has two nested optimization levels, matching the answer's core architecture.
Confirms a unified modular MDO framework integrating disciplinary modules was implemented for conceptual aircraft design.
Shows the upper nested level optimizes configuration geometric variables, supporting configuration optimization in the route.
Shows the upper nested level optimizes wing-box layout and wingtip/tip-chord variables.
Describes Level 1 performance optimizations, supporting the two-level nested optimization structure.
Reports static-margin enforcement raised gross weight about 6%, showing static-margin constraints materially change optimized design.
Shows plate-buckling constraints were included, supporting structural constraints in the MDO problem.
Finds the wing box was primarily sized by plate-buckling constraints, supporting structural constraints materially affecting design.
Limits the structural-constraint claim: this MDO problem omitted stress and displacement constraints.
Shows the displacement constraint was inactive, bounding which structural constraints materially affect this design.
Specifies the coupled 35-equation nonlinear DAE with 39 variables and 30 parameters.
Gives a wind-axis force equation, showing axis-system equation structure for flight simulation.
Gives a wind-axis scalar equation, supporting velocity-axis formulation of flight dynamics.
Gives a wind-axis angle-of-attack equation, supporting axis-system simulation equations.
Expresses body-axis angular rates from Euler angles, specifying state-variable relation.
Provides body-axis rotational acceleration equations, supporting six-DOF equation structure.
States forward-simulation input variables needed for a unique solution.
Constrains input specification to inverse-simulation mode with trajectory coordinates plus one variable.
Limits reduced moment equations to left-right symmetric airplanes.
Describes real-time simulation computing aircraft dynamics differential equations.
Reports estimating a delta aerodynamic model from flight data for simulation updating.
Gives identified ΔC_X delta-model parameters from flight-test maneuvers.
Gives identified ΔC_Z delta-model parameters from flight-test maneuvers.
Gives identified ΔC_m delta-model parameters from flight-test maneuvers.
Describes estimated delta aerodynamic models for longitudinal coefficients used to update simulation.
States augmented aerodynamic database significantly improves flight-parameter predictions.
Reports independent flight-test validation of the updated model's improvement.
Shows updated model closely matches measured angle of attack, pitch, and altitude.
Shows original model deviates from measured flight profiles, motivating data-based calibration.
Describes parameter identification from simulated elevator-doublet data reproducing longitudinal coefficients.
Ground computer solving aircraft dynamics each cycle directly instantiates the real-time HIL computational core.
HIL system running stably before flight test directly supports pre-flight validation.
Engine control with specified permissible tracking errors directly supports tracking-error validation in HIL.
Integrated flight control and propulsion operating effectively supports exercising integrated systems in HIL validation.
Reported attitude stability in joint HIL supports validation via stability results.
Successful reference trajectory tracking in joint HIL supports validation via tracking results.
Closed-loop HIL platform integrating flight control, propulsion, simulation equipment, and database supports the validation route.
Hardware set including flight control computer, engine controller/simulator, and ground computer supports HIL validation setup.
Low-cost workflow combining dynamics model, autopilot, and SITL/HITL testing supports HIL validation as a method.
HIL-versus-flight discrepancies around 10% bound the fidelity/accuracy claim for HIL validation.

details.content: One of the three scalar wind‑axis equations, in the wind axes (velocity‑aligned axes), is $$ \begin{aligned} m\dot{V} &= \bar{q}S\!\left(C_x\cos\alpha\cos\beta + C_y\sin\beta + C_z\sin\alpha\cos\beta\right) \\ &\quad + m g_0(\cos\theta\sin\phi\sin\beta-\sin\theta\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\theta\cos\phi\sin\alpha\cos\beta)+T\cos\alpha\cos\beta, \end{aligned} $$ with $m$ mass, $V$ speed, $\alpha$ angle of attack, $\beta$ sideslip, $\rho$ air density, $\theta$ pitch angle, $\phi$ roll angle, $\bar{q}=0.5\rho V^2$ dynamic pressure, $S$ wing area, $C_x,C_y,C_z$ body‑axis aerodynamic force coefficients, $g_0$ gravitational acceleration, $T$ thrust, and $p,q,r$ body angular rates.

details.content: The rotational dynamics for a generic asymmetric aircraft are given as three differential equations for the body angular acceleration components $(\dot{p},\dot{q},\dot{r})$ in terms of the inertia determinant $T_0$ and auxiliary moment quantities $(T_1,T_2,T_3)$; the equation for the body angular acceleration component $\dot{p}$ is $T_0\dot{p} = (BC - D^2)T_1 + (FC + ED)T_2 + (FD + EB)T_3$, where the inertia determinant is $T_0 = ABC - A D^2 - B E^2 - C F^2 - 2 D E F$, where $A=I_{xx}, B=I_{yy}, C=I_{zz}, D=I_{yz}, E=I_{xz}, F=I_{xy}$, the auxiliary moments are $T_1 = (B-C)qr + (E q - F r)p + (q^2-r^2)D + L$, $T_2 = (C-A)rp + (F r - D p)q + (r^2-p^2)E + M$, and $T_3 = (A-B)pq + (D p - E q)r + (p^2-q^2)F + N$, where $L,M,N$ are the aerodynamic moments about the body axes $x_b$, $y_b$, $z_b$ respectively.

details.content: For a hypothetical fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) with maximum take-off weight 115 kg, wing area 4.0 m^2, mean aerodynamic chord 0.63 m, span 6.34 m, engine power 20 hp, and propeller diameter 34 in, trimmed at an altitude of 1000 m and an airspeed of 80 knots, the unified six-degree-of-freedom model and its linearized longitudinal state-space representation are used to simulate the response to a prescribed elevator-deflection input, with longitudinal aerodynamic coefficients obtained from the USAF Stability and Control Digital DATCOM (DATCOM) and handbook methods. The nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom model produces time histories of the state variables $u$ (axial velocity), $w$ (vertical velocity), $\theta$ (pitch angle), $q$ (pitch rate), and altitude variation $\Delta h$, and of the output variables true airspeed $V$, altitude $H$, angle of attack $\alpha$, and accelerations $a_x$, $a_z$. The linearized longitudinal state-space model, when simulated for the same elevator input, yields an open-loop response that is compared with the nonlinear behavior.

The linearized longitudinal state-space model, when simulated for the same elevator input, yields an open-loop response that is compared with the nonlinear behavior.

details.content: For a 115 kg fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) trimmed at 1000 m altitude and 80 knots, the open-loop responses to elevator deflection show that the phugoid mode of the linearized longitudinal small-perturbation state-space model dominates, causing low-frequency, lightly damped behaviour in nearly all variables.

details.content: The thrust coefficient definition $C_T = T/(\rho n^2 D^4)$, with $T$ the thrust and $\rho$ the air density, with the body-axis force coefficient normalization, in which the thrust force is divided by the freestream dynamic pressure $\bar{q} = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2$ and the wing reference area $S$, yields the propulsion component of the body x-axis force coefficient $C_{T_x,\mathrm{prop}} = 2(D^2/S)(C_{T0}J^2 + C_{T1}J + C_{T2})$, where $C_T = C_{T0} + C_{T1}J_{adv} + C_{T2}J_{adv}^2$, $J_{adv} = V/(nD)$ is the advance ratio, and $J = nD/V$ is the inverse-advance-ratio quantity.

details.content: In a controlled comparison using identical polynomial model structures fitted to the CZ-150 body x-axis force coefficient $C_{T_x}$, where $J = nD/V$ and $J_{adv} = V/(nD)$ with $V$ the true airspeed, $n$ the propulsor rotational speed, and $D$ the propeller diameter, the centered inverse-advance-ratio variable $\bar{J} = J - 2$ produced a significantly better fit to the identification flight data than the centered advance-ratio variable $\bar{J}_{adv} = J_{adv} - 0.5$, with a higher coefficient of determination $R^2$ and a normalized root-mean-square error that was 3.8 times lower.

search_documents.text: KEACDE (Knowledge‑based and Extensible Aircraft Conceptual Design Environment) is implemented as a web‑based basic suite whose architecture is organized in two levels: (a) the KEACDE basic suite comprising a Knowledge Component Engine and an Extensible Basic Database and (b) higher‑level conceptual design systems constructed from the basic suite.
search_documents.title: P1

search_documents.text: The Knowledge Component Engine (KCE) provides a knowledge wrapper that enables designers to package engineering knowledge into modular "knowledge components", which contain (i) a hierarchical product data description of the design object and (ii) the methods and tools that generate or analyze that product data.
search_documents.title: P2

search_documents.text: The Knowledge Component Engine (KCE) exposes non‑programming wrapping tools: a "contents manager" to define hierarchical geometric and non‑geometric product descriptions and a "flexible extension tool" that wraps external algorithms, in‑house programs or commercial CAD/CAE software by parsing input/output files, driving programs, and by using COM interfaces or script parsing for secondary development.
search_documents.title: P3

search_documents.text: Packaged knowledge components, which contain (i) a hierarchical product data description of the design object and (ii) the methods and tools that generate or analyze that product data, are published to and retrieved from a web knowledge server
search_documents.title: P4

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database is a web‑based, browser/server database framework that enables designers to construct hierarchical databases for conceptual design without programming.
search_documents.title: P5

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database (EBD) supports definition and modification of hierarchical node structures, configuration of node attributes, data import/export and template management, keyword and structured searching, hierarchical and file/model/picture/video viewing, and basic numeric/character/file/model data analysis and chart/report generation.
search_documents.title: P6

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database (EBD) accepts numeric, character, file, model , picture and video data
search_documents.title: P7

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database (EBD) was used to instantiate built‑in libraries
search_documents.title: P8

search_documents.text: A built‑in, web‑based Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System was developed using the Knowledge‑based and Extensible Aircraft Conceptual Design Environment.
search_documents.title: P9

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) implements a three‑level architecture.
search_documents.title: P10

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database (EBD) of the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) constructed basic databases.
search_documents.title: P11

search_documents.text: The Knowledge Component Engine (KCE) of the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) wrapped design and analysis components.
search_documents.title: P12

search_documents.text: A management layer of the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) coordinates multidisciplinary design optimization and data management.
search_documents.title: P13

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) exposes a parametric product data description for civil airplanes comprising geometry, propulsion, aerodynamics, weight, flight performance and cost in a hierarchical structure.
search_documents.title: P14

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) provides a workflow from parametric geometry modeling through analysis to optimization under a unified operating and integration framework.
search_documents.title: P15

search_documents.text: CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) supplies parametric geometric modeling tools.
search_documents.title: P16

search_documents.text: CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) supports fuselage modeling, multi‑section wing modeling, empennage/nacelle modeling, cabin configuration, landing gear geometry/layout, and engine/equipment layout.
search_documents.title: P17

search_documents.text: The CATIA integration is achieved by the flexible extension tool, a non‑programming wrapping tool that parses input/output files and drives programs via Component Object Model (COM) interfaces or script parsing for secondary development, enabling non‑programmer designers to drive CATIA for model generation within CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System).
search_documents.title: P18

search_documents.text: CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) integrates weight estimation and center‑of‑gravity calculation modules.
search_documents.title: P19

search_documents.text: The weight estimator wraps the AAA weight calculation algorithm with added capabilities for chart/report generation.
search_documents.title: P20

search_documents.text: The weight estimator can compute structure weight from CATIA models via CATIA's weight‑calculation Application Programming Interface.
search_documents.title: P21

search_documents.text: The CoG (center‑of‑gravity) module is a CATIA‑based secondary development tool that computes the model CoG for the parameterized geometry produced by CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System).
search_documents.title: P22

search_documents.text: Configuration and model parameters are passed automatically from the geometry module to the weight and CoG (center‑of‑gravity) calculations.
search_documents.title: P23

search_documents.text: CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) integrates two aerodynamic analysis levels to balance speed and fidelity in conceptual design.
search_documents.title: P24

search_documents.text: The first aerodynamic analysis level of CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) is an in‑house engineering‑algorithm program named ASAero for rapid estimates based on engineering correlations and database interpolation, requiring only basic aircraft parameters and providing fast analysis.
search_documents.title: P25

search_documents.text: The second aerodynamic analysis level of CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) is the higher‑order panel method PANAIR for medium‑fidelity potential‑flow analysis, requiring medium model detail and providing medium analysis speed.
search_documents.title: P26

search_documents.text: CACDS (Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System) defines the aerodynamic targets to be computed as the lift coefficient $C_{L}$, drag coefficient $C_{D}$, lift curve slope $C_{L\alpha}$, maximum lift coefficient $C_{L\text{max}}$, zero‑lift drag coefficient $C_{D0}$, and the lift‑to‑drag ratio $C_{L}/C_{D}$ as functions of Mach number and altitude.
search_documents.title: P27

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System wraps and integrates a flight performance analysis tool STARPerform, and a cost estimation tool STARCost.
search_documents.title: P28

search_documents.text: STARPerform, a flight performance analysis tool, is based on classical flight‑performance algorithms.
search_documents.title: P29

search_documents.text: STARCost, a cost estimation tool, amends the AAA cost algorithm.
search_documents.title: P30

search_documents.text: STARCost, a cost estimation tool, employs Roskam's parametric direct operating cost model.
search_documents.title: P31

search_documents.text: Both a flight performance analysis tool STARPerform and a cost estimation tool STARCost receive required inputs automatically from The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) modules.
search_documents.title: P32

search_documents.text: Both a flight performance analysis tool STARPerform and a cost estimation tool STARCost receive required inputs automatically from The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) modules, enabling rapid computation of performance metrics and cost outputs.
search_documents.title: P33

search_documents.text: STARCost, a cost estimation tool, computes direct operating cost (DOC) components per Roskam's parametric direct operating cost model.
search_documents.title: P34

search_documents.text: STARCost, a cost estimation tool, reports results in consistent units for optimization.
search_documents.title: P35

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) is coupled with ModelCenter, a simulation integration and design optimization environment, as the optimization engine by treating CACDS as a functional component with defined input and output files.
search_documents.title: P36

search_documents.text: The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) parses input/output to expose design variables, constraints and objectives to ModelCenter, a simulation integration and design optimization environment.
search_documents.title: P37

search_documents.text: ModelCenter, a simulation integration and design optimization environment, includes prebuilt optimization templates saved as ModelCenter .pxc files.
search_documents.title: P38

search_documents.text: ModelCenter, a simulation integration and design optimization environment, supports Design of Experiments ‑based sensitivity analysis workflows.
search_documents.title: P39

search_documents.text: The demonstration case (the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane) uses the Boeing Design Explorer optimizer and full factorial Design of Experiments (DOE) to compute main effects.
search_documents.title: P40

search_documents.text: The CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) demonstrates the environment end‑to‑end.
search_documents.title: P41

search_documents.text: In the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), geometry was created in CATIA format via CACDS.

search_documents.text: In the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), automated analyses produced the following representative results: weight breakdown: Maximum take‑off weight $=73\,804.94\ \mathrm{kg}$, Operational empty weight $=37\,739.01\ \mathrm{kg}$ (51.13%), Structure weight $=17\,151.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ (23.24%), Fuel weight $=18\,496.36\ \mathrm{kg}$ (25.06%), Wing weight $=4\,435.183\ \mathrm{kg}$ (6.009%), Fuselage weight $=6\,118.123\ \mathrm{kg}$ (8.289%).
search_documents.title: P43

search_documents.text: For the CJX 150-seat single-aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), the cost outputs included a life cycle cost of 115,288.01×10^6 dollars, a Research Development Test Evaluation (RDTE) cost of 1,380.97×10^6 dollars, an acquisition cost of 9,435.65×10^6 dollars, an operating cost of 103,316.43×10^6 dollars, and a direct operating cost (DOC) of 15.92 dollar·nm⁻¹.
search_documents.title: P44

search_documents.text: For the CJX 150-seat civil airplane case, aerodynamic evaluation with PANAIR found a wing maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 34.55 at an angle of attack of 2.51°, Mach number Ma = 0.78, and altitude 11 km.
search_documents.title: P45

search_documents.text: In the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), a Direct operating cost (DOC)‑minimization optimization using ModelCenter's (a simulation integration and design optimization environment) Boeing Design Explorer optimizer over seven wing geometric design variables (spanwise lengths, taper ratios, and sweeps of inboard and outboard wing segments, and wing root chord length) with constraints on wing loading and drag coefficient completed in 93 runs and reduced Direct operating cost (DOC) from $15.9191$ to $15.6183\ \text{dollar·nm}^{-1}$.
search_documents.title: P46

search_documents.text: For the CJX 150-seat civil airplane case, the optimized concept after DOC-minimization optimization using ModelCenter's Boeing Design Explorer optimizer had an inboard wing span of 5.2 m (initial 6.412 m), an outboard wing span of 9 m (initial 9.84 m), inboard sweep of 22° (initial 27.39°), outboard sweep of 22° (initial 27.39°), wing root chord of 7.02 m (initial 6.921 m), inboard taper ratio of 0.596563 (initial 0.52), and outboard taper ratio of 0.3 (initial 0.406).
search_documents.title: P47

search_documents.text: In the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), sensitivity analysis using Design of Experiments (DOE) with a full factorial design computed main effects (defined as the change in Direct operating cost (DOC) with respect to each design variable).
search_documents.title: P48

search_documents.text: Among the seven wing geometric design variables (spanwise lengths, taper ratios, and sweeps of inboard and outboard wing segments, and wing root chord length), spanwise lengths of the inboard and outboard wing segments and outboard sweep are the most influential variables with main effects (defined as the change in Direct operating cost (DOC) with respect to each design variable) of 29%, 32%, and 16% respectively.
search_documents.title: P49

search_documents.text: The Extensible Basic Database (EBD) supports definition and modification of hierarchical node structures, configuration of node attributes, data import/export and template management, keyword and structured searching, hierarchical and file/CATIA/picture/video viewing, and basic numeric/character/file/CATIA data analysis and chart/report generation.

search_documents.title: P52

search_documents.text: The Knowledge Component Engine (KCE) of the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) wrapped the six design and analysis components: geometry modeling, weight, aerodynamics, propulsion, flight performance, and cost.

search_documents.title: P55

search_documents.text: Both a flight performance analysis tool STARPerform and a cost estimation tool STARCost receive required inputs automatically from The Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS) modules, enabling rapid computation of the takeoff, climb, descent, landing and cruise performance metrics and the life‑cycle and DOC cost outputs.
search_documents.title: P56

search_documents.text: ModelCenter, a simulation integration and design optimization environment, includes the direct Direct Operating Cost minimization template, the flight‑performance optimization template, and the aero‑weight multi‑objective templates saved as ModelCenter .pxc files.
search_documents.title: P57

search_documents.text: In the CJX 150‑seat single‑aisle civil airplane design case implemented in the Civil Airplane Conceptual Design System (CACDS), a Direct operating cost (DOC)‑minimization optimization using ModelCenter's (a simulation integration and design optimization environment) Boeing Design Explorer optimizer over seven wing geometric design variables (spanwise lengths, taper ratios, and sweeps of inboard and outboard wing segments, and wing root chord length) with constraints on the wing loading in the range 540–620 kg·m⁻² and the drag coefficient below 0.01521 completed in 93 runs and reduced Direct operating cost (DOC) from $15.9191$ to $15.6183\ \text{dollar·nm}^{-1}$.
search_documents.title: P58

search_documents.text: A unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design was implemented that integrates the main aircraft disciplinary modules into a single optimization environment
search_documents.title: P59

search_documents.text: The implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design includes a Program Core that manages data flow between modules and interfaces and is accessible via a graphical user interface, by command line, or by other software through Windows dynamic-link libraries.
search_documents.title: P60

search_documents.text: The implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design supports two nested optimization levels.
search_documents.title: P61

search_documents.text: Level 1 (the Performance Module) of the two nested optimization levels supported by the implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design performs single-level optimizations over control design variables for a fixed aircraft configuration.
search_documents.title: P62

search_documents.text: Level 2 (the Optimization Module) of the two nested optimization levels supported by the implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design optimizes configuration geometric design variables while including the objective functions and constraints of Level 1 (the Performance Module) so that configuration-level decisions account for optimized control/morphing strategies.
search_documents.title: P63

search_documents.text: For the Embraer™-based regional-jet reference model designated EMB9MOR used in the study, adding and optimizing a rigid wingtip increased calculated cruise range R from 5458.88 km for the baseline without wingtip to 5996.06 km for the aircraft with the optimized wingtip.
search_documents.title: P64

search_documents.text: For the Embraer™-based regional-jet reference model designated EMB9MOR used in the study, adding and optimizing a rigid wingtip reduced cruise fuel consumption by approximately 8% for the cruise condition.
search_documents.title: P65

search_documents.text: For the Embraer™-based regional-jet reference model designated EMB9MOR used in the study, adding and optimizing a rigid wingtip reduced climb throttle requirement corresponding to approximately 13% fuel-consumption reduction for the climb condition.
search_documents.title: P66

search_documents.text: For the Embraer™-based regional-jet reference model designated EMB9MOR used in the study, the wing structural mass increased from 1502.63 kg (no wingtip) to 1913.81 kg (with wingtip).
search_documents.title: P67

search_documents.text: Allowing the wingtip to morph between cruise and climb by optimizing wingtip control parameters (toe θ_{wt}, cant Γ_{wt}, sweep Λ_{wt}) and optionally geometric parameters (span b_{wt}, tip chord c_{wt}) produced only marginal additional fuel savings relative to a wingtip optimized for cruise and held fixed during climb.
search_documents.title: P68

search_documents.text: the computed differential fuel-consumption improvement was below 1% overall and about 0.5% in climb for the tested cases;

search_documents.title: P70

search_documents.text: The omission of the mass or complexity of morphing actuators and mechanisms from the multidisciplinary sizing and mission optimization reported would, if included, be expected to eliminate or reverse the sub‑1% aerodynamic-only benefit reported in claim 13. [Referenced claim 13: the computed differential fuel-consumption improvement was below 1% overall and about 0.5% in climb for the tested cases;]
search_documents.title: P71

search_documents.text: For the joined‑wing reference configuration evaluated at low speed (V = 30 m/s) and sea level altitude, optimizing a bending‑and‑twist morphing wingtip—parameterized by symmetric and anti‑symmetric tip bending amplitudes and a linear twist distribution from root to tip—produced large increases in the yaw moment coefficient C_n relative to the clean (unmorphed) configuration.
search_documents.title: P72

search_documents.text: ( C_n rising from 0.0029 clean to up to 0.0216 for a high‑amplitude symmetric morphing case and to 0.0151 for a more conservative morphed case)
search_documents.title: P73

search_documents.text: For the joined‑wing reference configuration evaluated at low speed (V = 30 m/s) and sea level altitude, optimizing a bending‑and‑twist morphing wingtip—parameterized by symmetric and anti‑symmetric tip bending amplitudes and a linear twist distribution from root to tip—reduces the predicted time T to achieve a 60° heading change under the constant‑acceleration assumption from T = 1.88 s (clean) to approximately T ≈ 0.69–0.82 s for the morphed configurations.
search_documents.title: P74

search_documents.text: For the joined‑wing reference configuration evaluated at low speed (V = 30 m/s) and sea level altitude, replacing outboard conventional ailerons with the morphing tip control yielded substantially lower roll moment coefficient C_l.
search_documents.title: P75

search_documents.text: (clean with ailerons C_l = 0.0462 versus morphing cases with C_l in the range 0.0085–0.0150)
search_documents.title: P76

search_documents.text: For the joined‑wing reference configuration evaluated at low speed (V = 30 m/s) and sea level altitude, replacing outboard conventional ailerons with the morphing tip control yielded reduced roll authority.
search_documents.title: P77

search_documents.text: For the joined‑wing reference configuration evaluated at low speed (V = 30 m/s) and sea level altitude, replacing outboard conventional ailerons with the morphing tip control yielded slower bank response.
search_documents.title: P78

search_documents.text: ( bank‑change times of T = 0.47 s clean versus T ≥ 0.83 s for the morphing cases under the same constant‑acceleration assumption)
search_documents.title: P79

search_documents.text: Level 1 (the Performance Module) of the two nested optimization levels supported by the implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design performs single-level optimizations over angle of attack α, engine throttle setting proportional to fuel flow, and the morphing control parameters wingtip toe angle θ_{wt}, cant Γ_{wt}, and sweep Λ_{wt} for a fixed aircraft configuration.
search_documents.title: P80

search_documents.text: Level 2 (the Optimization Module) of the two nested optimization levels supported by the implementation of a unified, modular Multidisciplinary Design Optimization framework for conceptual aircraft design optimizes internal wing box layout parameters, wingtip span b_{wt}, and tip chord c_{wt} while including the objective functions and constraints of Level 1 (the Performance Module) so that configuration-level decisions account for optimized control/morphing strategies.
search_documents.title: P81

search_documents.text: The closed, time-domain ordinary differential equation (ODE) state-space model formulated for take-off and landing maneuvers in a vertical plane includes ground rolling friction $\mu(W-L)$, ground-effect scaling of induced drag, distinct on-ground and airborne force balances, and a well-posed initial value problem for a prescribed $u(t)$ and initial state.
search_documents.title: P82

search_documents.text: During braking in a rejected take-off, the longitudinal acceleration becomes $f_2(\boldsymbol{x},u)=\dfrac{g}{W}\{-D(x_2,u)-\mu_{\mathrm{brakes}}[W-L(x_2,u)]\}$.

search_documents.title: P86

search_documents.text: A MATLAB/Simulink-based modeling and simulation framework was developed that enables (ii) modeling and simulation of dynamics of propulsion, energy, and control actuation systems.
search_documents.title: P87

search_documents.text: A MATLAB/Simulink-based modeling and simulation framework was developed that enables (iii) convenient interfacing with aero-propulsive databases generated using external tools.
search_documents.title: P88

search_documents.title: P92

search_documents.text: A vectorized Blade Element Momentum Theory (BEMT) code is executed at the simulation timestep using $n_{rad} \times n_{azi} \times 6$ matrices (where $n_{rad}$ and $n_{azi}$ are the number of radial and azimuthal divisions of each rotor) for computational efficiency, enabling real-time operation with a 1/60 s timestep on a laptop.

search_documents.title: P96

search_documents.text: The Total Energy Control System (TECS) for longitudinal control was verified on the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 (HCPAV-V1).
search_documents.title: P97

search_documents.text: In a simulation where the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 (HCPAV-V1) was initially trimmed at 30 knots and a velocity step command to 50 knots was applied at t=15 s, the Total Energy Control System (TECS) controller produced a simultaneous increase in $N_0$ (collective) and $N_\theta$ (longitudinal cyclic, nose-down pitch).
search_documents.title: P98

search_documents.text: In a simulation where the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 (HCPAV-V1) was initially trimmed at 30 knots and a velocity step command to 50 knots was applied at t=15 s, the $\dot{E}$ and $\dot{L}$ time histories, where $\dot{E} = \frac{\dot{V}}{g} + \gamma$ and $\dot{L} = \frac{\dot{V}}{g} - \gamma$, with $V$ the true airspeed, $g$ the acceleration due to gravity, and $\gamma$ the flightpath angle, were close but not identical, resulting in a small flightpath coupling.
search_documents.title: P99

search_documents.text: In a simulation where the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 (HCPAV-V1) was initially trimmed at 30 knots and a velocity step command to 50 knots was applied at t=15 s, the altitude excursion during the maneuver was limited to approximately 1 m.
search_documents.title: P100

search_documents.text: In a simulation, the commanded headings were attained satisfactorily through smooth bank angle changes.
search_documents.title: P101

search_documents.text: In a simulation, sideslip angle excursions were present.
search_documents.title: P102

search_documents.text: In a simulation, sideslip angle excursions were damped by the Total Heading Control System (THCS) controller.
search_documents.title: P103

search_documents.text: In a simulation, velocity excursions were limited to approximately ±1 knot.
search_documents.title: P104

search_documents.text: In a simulation, altitude excursions were within a 1.5 m window.
search_documents.title: P105

search_documents.text: During banks in a simulation, $N_0$ (collective) increased.
search_documents.title: P106

search_documents.text: During banks in a simulation, $N_\theta$ (longitudinal cyclic) reduced (nose-up pitch).

search_documents.text: In a simulation, a lateral velocity step command of 3 knots was applied at t=5 s and removed at t=20 s.

search_documents.text: In a simulation, the front and aft vanes of the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 deflected in opposite directions to produce the necessary yawing moments to start and stop the pure yaw rotation during hover.

search_documents.text: In a simulation, the response showed that the yaw rate tracking controller effectively commanded the opposing vane deflections of the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 1 to achieve the heading changes, a $90^\circ$ heading change to the right at t=5 s and a $90^\circ$ turn back to the original heading at t=20 s.

search_documents.text: The axis tilt angle command $\delta_{axis}$ is generated by slowly integrating the pitch attitude command: $\delta_{axis}(s) = \left(K_{axis}/s\right)\theta_{cmd}(s)$, where $K_{axis}$ is a proportional gain, $s$ is the Laplace variable, and $\theta_{cmd}$ is the commanded pitch attitude; this approach allows the pitch attitude of the Hexa-Chakra Personal Air Vehicle version 2 (HCPAV-V2) model to return to zero over the full range of forward speeds.
search_documents.title: P120

search_documents.text: The axis tilt angle command $\delta_{axis}$ is generated by slowly integrating the pitch attitude command: $\delta_{axis}(s) = \left(K_{axis}/s\right)\theta_{cmd}(s)$, where $K_{axis}$ is a proportional gain, $s$ is the Laplace variable, and $\theta_{cmd}$ is the commanded pitch attitude; this approach is eliminating the significant nose-down trim observed in HCPAV-V1 at higher speeds.
search_documents.title: P121

search_documents.text: The delta aerodynamic model for the longitudinal coefficients \(C_X\) (force coefficient in the \(x\)-direction), \(C_Z\) (force coefficient in the \(z\)-direction), and \(C_m\) (moment coefficient about the \(y\)-axis), which was estimated for a 450 kg, tail-controlled, gliding autonomous air vehicle using stepwise regression on flight test data from four maneuvers, corrects the prior aerodynamic database by adding polynomial functions of angle of attack (\(\alpha\)), Mach number, pitch rate (\(q\)), elevator deflection (\(\delta_e\)), and their interactions.
search_documents.title: P122

search_documents.text: The estimated parameters and their 95% confidence bounds for the delta aerodynamic model of the longitudinal coefficient ΔC_X, which was estimated for a 450 kg, tail-controlled, gliding autonomous air vehicle using stepwise regression on flight test data from four maneuvers, are an α^3 term of 57.120 ± 1.136 and a static term of −0.034 ± 0.004.
search_documents.title: P123

search_documents.text: The estimated parameters and their 95% confidence bounds for the delta aerodynamic model of the longitudinal coefficient ΔC_Z, which was estimated for a 450 kg, tail-controlled, gliding autonomous air vehicle using stepwise regression on flight test data from four maneuvers, are terms in α of 13.803 ± 1.098, Mach of −2.146 ± 0.073, q of 1184.722 ± 79.434, α^2 of −101.988 ± 10.910, and a static term of 1.865 ± 0.095.
search_documents.title: P124

search_documents.text: The estimated parameters and their 95% confidence bounds for the delta aerodynamic model of the longitudinal coefficient ΔC_m, which was estimated for a 450 kg, tail-controlled, gliding autonomous air vehicle using stepwise regression on flight test data from four maneuvers, are terms in Mach of 1.188 ± 0.123, δ_e of 34.716 ± 1.644, α·δ_e of 209.064 ± 5.396, and a static term of 0.522 ± 0.163.
search_documents.title: P125

search_documents.text: The delta aerodynamic model for the longitudinal coefficients \(C_X\) (force coefficient in the \(x\)-direction), \(C_Z\) (force coefficient in the \(z\)-direction), and \(C_m\) (moment coefficient about the \(y\)-axis), which was estimated for a 450 kg, tail-controlled, gliding autonomous air vehicle using stepwise regression on flight test data from four maneuvers, reproduces the aerodynamic coefficients \(C_X\), \(C_Z\), and \(C_m\) calculated from the four estimation maneuvers with good fidelity.

search_documents.text: One of the three scalar wind‑axis equations, in the wind axes (velocity‑aligned axes), is $$ \begin{aligned} m\dot{V} &= \bar{q}S\!\left(C_x\cos\alpha\cos\beta + C_y\sin\beta + C_z\sin\alpha\cos\beta\right) \\ &\quad + m g_0(\cos\theta\sin\phi\sin\beta-\sin\theta\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\theta\cos\phi\sin\alpha\cos\beta)+T\cos\alpha\cos\beta, \end{aligned} $$ with $m$ mass, $V$ speed, $\alpha$ angle of attack, $\beta$ sideslip, $\rho$ air density, $\theta$ pitch angle, $\phi$ roll angle, $\bar{q}=0.5\rho V^2$ dynamic pressure, $S$ wing area, $C_x,C_y,C_z$ body‑axis aerodynamic force coefficients, $g_0$ gravitational acceleration, $T$ thrust, and $p,q,r$ body angular rates.

search_documents.text: The rotational dynamics for a generic asymmetric aircraft are given as three differential equations for the body angular acceleration components $(\dot{p},\dot{q},\dot{r})$ in terms of the inertia determinant $T_0$ and auxiliary moment quantities $(T_1,T_2,T_3)$; the equation for the body angular acceleration component $\dot{p}$ is $T_0\dot{p} = (BC - D^2)T_1 + (FC + ED)T_2 + (FD + EB)T_3$, where the inertia determinant is $T_0 = ABC - A D^2 - B E^2 - C F^2 - 2 D E F$, where $A=I_{xx}, B=I_{yy}, C=I_{zz}, D=I_{yz}, E=I_{xz}, F=I_{xy}$, the auxiliary moments are $T_1 = (B-C)qr + (E q - F r)p + (q^2-r^2)D + L$, $T_2 = (C-A)rp + (F r - D p)q + (r^2-p^2)E + M$, and $T_3 = (A-B)pq + (D p - E q)r + (p^2-q^2)F + N$, where $L,M,N$ are the aerodynamic moments about the body axes $x_b$, $y_b$, $z_b$ respectively.

search_documents.text: An efficient flight experiment was designed and executed for aero-propulsive system identification of the CZ-150, a small fixed-wing unmanned aircraft with elevator, aileron, and rudder control surfaces and a single nose-mounted electric motor driving a two-bladed 16x8-in. propeller, in which orthogonal, phase-optimized multisine input signals were applied simultaneously to the control surfaces and the propulsion system, allowing identification of integrated propulsion and airframe aerodynamics in a single maneuver.
search_documents.title: P248

search_documents.text: The multiple-input maneuver resulting from an efficient flight experiment in which orthogonal, phase-optimized multisine input signals were applied simultaneously to the control surfaces and the propulsion system produced decorrelated coverage of true airspeed $V$, propulsor rotational speed $n$, and the inverse advance ratio $J = nD/V$, where $D = 1.333$ ft is the propeller diameter.
search_documents.title: P249

search_documents.text: The inverse-advance-ratio quantity $J = nD/V$ is derived as the physically consistent primary dimensionless explanatory variable for representing propulsion effects in the conventional nondimensional body-axis aircraft force and moment coefficients.
search_documents.title: P250

search_documents.text: The thrust coefficient definition $C_T = T/(\rho n^2 D^4)$, with $T$ the thrust and $\rho$ the air density, with the body-axis force coefficient normalization, in which the thrust force is divided by the freestream dynamic pressure $\bar{q} = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2$ and the wing reference area $S$, yields the propulsion component of the body x-axis force coefficient $C_{T_x,\mathrm{prop}} = 2(D^2/S)(C_{T0}J^2 + C_{T1}J + C_{T2})$, where $C_T = C_{T0} + C_{T1}J_{adv} + C_{T2}J_{adv}^2$, $J_{adv} = V/(nD)$ is the advance ratio, and $J = nD/V$ is the inverse-advance-ratio quantity.
search_documents.title: P251

search_documents.text: The inverse-advance-ratio quantity $J = nD/V$ arises naturally from the correct propeller nondimensionalization.
search_documents.title: P252

search_documents.text: In a controlled comparison using identical polynomial model structures fitted to the CZ-150 body x-axis force coefficient $C_{T_x}$, where $J = nD/V$ and $J_{adv} = V/(nD)$ with $V$ the true airspeed, $n$ the propulsor rotational speed, and $D$ the propeller diameter, the centered inverse-advance-ratio variable $\bar{J} = J - 2$ produced a significantly better fit to the identification flight data than the centered advance-ratio variable $\bar{J}_{adv} = J_{adv} - 0.5$, with a higher coefficient of determination $R^2$ and a normalized root-mean-square error that was 3.8 times lower.
search_documents.title: P253

search_documents.text: $J = nD/V$ is the more appropriate propulsion modeling variable for aircraft force and moment coefficients than advance ratio $J_{adv} = V/(nD)$, with $V$ the true airspeed, $n$ the propulsor rotational speed, and $D$ the propeller diameter.

search_documents.text: $J = nD/V$ is consistent with the nondimensionalization of propeller aerodynamics rather than mixing propeller and airframe normalizations, with $V$ the true airspeed, $n$ the propulsor rotational speed, and $D$ the propeller diameter.

R1
search_documents.text: 集成概念设计环境 Integrated conceptual design environment Aircraft simulation design can be organized around an integrated conceptual-design and simulation-optimization environment that runs an end-to-end civil-airplane design case and uses an optimizer to minimize a design objective such as direct operating cost. Evidence would include claims showing an end-to-end conceptual design system and an optimization environment minimizing a design objective within that workflow.

search_documents.title: R2
search_documents.text: 嵌套多学科优化 Nested multidisciplinary optimization Conceptual aircraft design can be pursued through a unified modular multidisciplinary design optimization framework with nested optimization levels that optimize configuration and wing-box design variables, while structural and static-margin constraints may materially affect the resulting design. Evidence would include a modular MDO framework with nested optimization levels and studies showing how structural or static-margin constraints change optimized designs.

search_documents.title: R3
search_documents.text: 非线性飞行动力学建模 Nonlinear flight-dynamics formulation Aircraft simulation can be formulated as a coupled nonlinear differential-algebraic flight-dynamics model with six-degree-of-freedom equations expressed in body or wind axes, requiring state variables and parameters to be specified. Evidence would include claims specifying the DAE structure, axis-system equations, and variable or parameter requirements for flight-dynamics simulation.

search_documents.title: R4
search_documents.text: 飞行数据模型校正 Flight-data model calibration Simulation-model fidelity can be improved by identifying aerodynamic delta or parameter models from flight-test or simulated doublet data and updating the original aerodynamic database, followed by checking predictions against measured flight parameters. Evidence would include identification of aerodynamic increments or parameters from test data and reported improvement of simulation predictions after updating the model.

search_documents.title: R5
search_documents.text: 硬件在环验证 Hardware-in-the-loop validation Before flight test, aircraft simulation design can be validated through real-time hardware-in-the-loop testing in which a ground computer solves the aircraft dynamics and the integrated control and propulsion systems are exercised under specified tracking-error criteria. Evidence would include a real-time HIL system computing aircraft dynamics, integrated control or propulsion operation, and reported tracking or stability results supporting pre-flight evaluation.
